qrdBas-ae6817-d1e101.summary: Rubric for the third prologue question of Book 1.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e106.summary: States the question: whether God is the subject of theology.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e115.summary: First argument for the negative: Boethius (De trinitate) says a simple form cannot be a subject; God is utterly simple form.
claims: A simple form cannot be a subject.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e126.summary: Second argument: matter and end do not coincide numerically (Physics II); God is the end and efficient cause of this science, so not its matter (subject).
claims: Matter and end cannot coincide.
concepts: subject as matter of a science

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e138.summary: Third argument: God has no principles (being first), no integral parts (being simple), no subjective parts (being singular), and no attributes distinct from his essence; so by Posterior Analytics I he cannot be the subject of a science.
claims: A subject of science must have principles, parts, or attributes, which God lacks.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e158.summary: Fourth argument: one must presuppose of a science's subject what it is (Posterior Analytics I), but God has no quiddity (Avicenna, Metaphysics IV). Augustine (De civitate VIII) is cited for the opposite.
claims: The subject of a science must have a known quiddity.
God has no quiddity, per Avicenna.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e169.summary: For the affirmative: theology is discourse (ratio) about God, and a science is named after its subject. God is the principle of being, and so of knowability (Metaphysics II), so other things can be known through him. The paragraph ends by announcing the order of procedure.
claims: Theology is named after God as its subject.
God, as principle of being, is the principle of knowability.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e187.summary: First step of the plan: show the per se ratio of the first subject of a science and its conditions.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e194.summary: Second step: show that God is the subject in theology and how.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e199.summary: Third step: exclude others' opinions on this.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e205.summary: Fourth step: resolve the principal arguments. Then begins the first article: the ratio of the first subject of a science is that it is first known in the science, before all else, by twofold precognition (whether it is and what it is), under its proper, formal, and actual ratio.
claims: The first subject of a science is what is first known in it, by its proper formal and actual ratio.
Its existence and quiddity are precognized.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e221.summary: Proves the third part (that the subject is first known): in essentially ordered things there must be a first where the series stops (Metaphysics II), and everything in a per se unified science is essentially ordered in knowability, so it reduces to one simply first known, which can only be the subject.
claims: Essentially ordered items in a science reduce to one first known, the subject.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e239.summary: Further: everything known in a science (principles, conclusions, subject, subjective parts, attributes, causes, anything with per se relation to the subject) reduces to knowledge of the subject. Conclusions reduce to principles, principles to terms, and per se second-mode predicates to the subject. If the predicate is per se first-mode, the subject is still known first confusedly.
claims: All knowledge in a science reduces to knowledge of its subject.
Even with first-mode predicates, the subject is known first confusedly.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e268.summary: Explains that what is first known confusedly is the most specific species, not the definition or its parts, however more common. So knowledge of everything reduces to the subject first known confusedly, and the first condition, that the subject is first known and first occurs to the intellect, is established.
claims: The most specific species is what is first known confusedly.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e286.summary: Second condition: the subject is precognized in two ways, what its name means and whether it is, the latter not in the sense of actual existence but as an essence not repugnant to existing, not impossible like fictions, since there is no science of non-being. Of attributes one precognizes only the meaning of the name; of axioms, that they are true.
claims: Of the subject one must precognize its nominal meaning and its non-impossibility.
There is no science of impossible fictions.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e306.summary: Third condition: the subject must be known through its own ratio, not another's, else that other would be first and the subject. Hence some note that a relation cannot be the subject of a science, being known through its foundation, and likewise negations and privations, though this concerns others' difficulties more than the main point.
claims: The subject must be known through its own ratio.
Relations, negations, and privations cannot be subjects of a science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e336.summary: Fourth condition: the subject is known through a formal, not merely material, ratio, since nothing is first known through a material ratio.
claims: The subject is known through a formal ratio.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e345.summary: Fifth condition: through an actual, not potential, formal ratio, since act is prior to potency in cognition and potential being is known only through actual being (Metaphysics IX).
claims: The subject is known through an actual, not potential, ratio.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e361.summary: Concludes that the known subject virtually and effectively, or at least objectively, contains knowledge of everything else known in the science, as the principle of an essentially ordered series to which all other knowledge resolves; it contains first, depending on nothing else in its being known.
claims: The subject virtually contains all knowledge in its science.
The subject is independent in its knowability; all else depends on it.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e383.summary: Confirmation: as the first object of a power relates to the power, so the first object of a science to the science, and the first object causes. So whatever can be first known by the twofold precognition can be the subject of some science. Then introduces the conditions of the subject relative to the science.
claims: Whatever can be first known by twofold precognition can be the subject of a science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e401.summary: Conditions of the subject relative to the science. First, it specifies the science as first cause containing and measuring it, not intrinsically as a differentia but as an extrinsic cause. Nor does it specify precisely and adequately, since diverse habits can concern the same object; it specifies inadequately, as an equivocal extrinsic cause.
claims: The subject specifies a science as an extrinsic, not intrinsic, cause.
The subject does not specify a science adequately; several sciences can share a subject.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e430.summary: Second condition: the subject gives the science its unity, understood in the same way as specification (Posterior Analytics I).
claims: The subject gives a science its unity.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e442.summary: Third condition: the first subject gives the science its dignity or nobility (De anima I), as Aristotle says it is greater to know a little probably about nobler objects such as separate substances than much demonstratively about lesser ones. Hence the subject also gives the science its name.
claims: The subject confers nobility and name on a science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e462.summary: Fourth condition: the subject of the science is also the subject of its principles, immediate first-mode and mediate second-mode, since mediate principles reduce to immediate ones and those to terms, the first of which is the subject.
claims: The subject of a science is the subject of its principles.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e475.summary: Announces a comparison of agreements and differences between the first object of a habit or science and the first object of a power.
concepts: object of power and of habit

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e484.summary: First agreement: the first object of each terminates its act.
claims: The first object terminates the act of power and science alike.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e491.summary: Second agreement: the first object of each is adequate to it, since neither tends to anything except its first object or through its ratio.
claims: The first object is adequate to its power or science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e500.summary: Third agreement: when a power or science concerns many objects, each able to terminate an act by its own nature (each colour for sight), each can be a first object by primacy of immediacy, though not of adequation, while something common by predication (colour, being) is the adequate first object. But by this agreement such a habit would be one only generically or by order; a per se unified science has a single first subject by both primacies. So this agreement does not hold between a per se one power and a per se one science.
claims: Primacy of immediacy differs from primacy of adequation.
A per se unified science has one subject first by both primacies, unlike a power.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e551.summary: Fourth agreement: when a power or science concerns one thing by its proper ratio and others only through it, not through being in common.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e560.summary: Fifth agreement: when a common object by predication is assigned as adequate, it need not be adequate in moving or measuring the act, only in terminating it. For some, a relation can terminate an act of intellect or science without moving or measuring it, though contained under being.
claims: A common adequate object is adequate only in terminating, not in moving or measuring, the act.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e591.summary: Others say a relation cannot terminate an act first, though it can secondarily, and cannot measure. When a power or science concerns one thing by its proper ratio and others only through being, only that one is adequate in moving and measuring (or quasi, given that divine things are not measured or moved), while others terminate only secondarily. A difference: the first object has the ratio of mover relative to a power but of cause or measure (confirmation) relative to a habit or act.
claims: Objects move powers but cause or measure habits and acts.
Secondary objects terminate acts but never move or measure them.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e641.summary: Fourth: how 'matter' and 'subject' are taken in a science, by analogy with nature, since art imitates nature. In nature the subject has first formal act (substantial form) and is in potency to accidents, while matter lacks substantial form and is in potency to it. So the subject of a science has in itself the formal objective ratio by which it moves the intellect, or by which the science regards it, and is in potency to knowledge as quasi-accident, not as transmutable but as extrinsically denominable 'known'. 'Matter' lacks such a ratio and is regarded only through relation to the subject, as if putting on its objective form.
claims: The subject of a science, like a natural subject, has a first formal ratio and is in denominative potency to knowledge.
The 'matter' of a science is known only through its relation to the subject.
concepts: subject versus matter of a science

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e715.summary: A second exposition: the first object is called 'subject' because the first scientific knowledge belongs to it; it is precognized (whether and what) and in accidental potency to further knowledge of itself. Matter is whatever is not precognized but in potency to first and further knowledge, all through relation to the subject.
claims: The subject is precognized and in potency to further knowledge; matter is in potency to all knowledge.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e737.summary: A third exposition: 'subject' in a science is used metaphorically, by imagination, as if the act of science passed into the object as transitive acts do into external matter, though in truth it remains in the soul as its real subject. So the first object is called 'subject' and the rest 'matter', and 'object' is more proper than 'subject'. Ends the first article.
claims: Calling the object of a science its 'subject' is metaphorical.
Knowledge really inheres in the soul, not the object.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e764.summary: Second article: reports some who hold that the subject of theology is not God but divine being or divine thing in common. First: God does not contain under him universally everything treated in theology, whereas 'divine being' is common to all of it. Second: God is the subject of metaphysics (the Commentator, Physics I), so not of theology, else the two sciences would be one.
claims: Theology treats things not universally contained under God.
God is the subject of metaphysics, so cannot be theology's without merging the sciences.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e793.summary: Third argument for that view: as power to object, so science to subject; powers are assigned a common adequate object (colour or light for sight, being for intellect); so theology should be assigned a common subject, divine being, not God or something virtually containing its truths.
claims: Sciences, like powers, have common adequate objects.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e811.summary: Fourth argument: a science presupposes and does not demonstrate its subject (the Commentator with Avicenna), but theology proves God.
claims: A science does not prove its own subject, but theology proves God.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e827.summary: Others argue: as subject to subject, so science to science proportionally; being is the subject of metaphysics (Avicenna, Metaphysics I.3; Aristotle, Metaphysics IV); if God were theology's subject, theology would be subalternate to metaphysics (God being contained under being), making metaphysics nobler, which is false.
claims: If God were theology's subject, theology would be subalternate to metaphysics.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e847.summary: Further: God cannot be simply first known, since a wayfarer knows him only deductively from effects, but a subject must be first known.
claims: God is known by wayfarers only from effects, so he is not first known.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e863.summary: Against that opinion, an ad hominem first: its proponent says in his Summa that God is the subject of theology.
claims: The proponent of 'divine being' elsewhere affirms God as theology's subject.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e875.summary: Second: when something common by predication is assigned as subject, like being in metaphysics, it must belong formally and intrinsically to everything positive considered in the science; but 'divine being' does not belong so to creatures, only to God.
claims: A common subject must belong formally to everything treated in the science.
Creatures are not formally divine beings.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e895.summary: Third: theological attributes such as being first and one do not properly belong to 'divine being' taken commonly across everything treated in theology.
claims: Proper theological attributes do not belong to divine being in common.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e904.summary: Fourth: no common notion virtually contains all theological truths, since it would then contain proper divine truths and place them in creatures where the common notion is found.
claims: No common concept virtually contains the proper truths about God.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e917.summary: Fifth: 'divine' so taken seems only a name taken from the agent and is predicated of everything like 'being', convertible with it; so being would be theology's subject, which is false. The paragraph's last words begin the author's statement.
claims: 'Divine being' taken broadly is convertible with being.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e933.summary: The author's statement: 'divine being', taken as they do and extended improperly to all things denominated from God, is not the subject. But taken properly and formally, as that to which deity belongs intrinsically and quidditatively, it is the subject, and this is God.
claims: Divine being in the proper sense, that to which deity belongs quidditatively, is God and is theology's subject.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e949.summary: To show God is the subject, first distinguishes theology in itself from theology for us. Theology in itself is the knowledge naturally apt to be had of the theological object by an intellect proportioned to it, evident from the object, whether intuitive (God's and the blessed's) or abstractive (shown possible to a wayfarer). Theology for us is what masters and doctors commonly have in this state.
claims: Theology in itself is evident knowledge of God by a proportioned intellect.
Theology for us is the knowledge actually available in this state.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e989.summary: Second distinction by parts: each theology has a part concerning necessary truths (God is triune) and a part concerning contingent truths (God created). A doctor (Scotus) illustrates the first distinction: one who cannot see geometry evidently but assents with certainty has 'faith' in geometry, while evident geometry is science in itself even if no one has it. The two theologies are not the same knowledge, else one intellect would know the same object evidently and inevidently, a contradiction. Nor is theology in itself had by no one, since what is in itself can be in another. They differ in that the first is naturally apt to be had evidently by a proportioned intellect and the second is commonly had in this state.
claims: Theology has parts about necessary truths and about contingent truths.
Theology in itself and theology for us are distinct knowledges.
Theology in itself is apt to be had evidently; theology for us is commonly had.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1076.summary: Conclusion: God is the subject of theology in itself concerning necessary truths, which is science in itself. First proof: what first and adequately, and alone, contains intelligibly all truths of a habit is its first subject; God virtually contains all necessary theological truths, and nothing else does, neither as cause (God has none), nor as something to which they are attributed, nor as effect (effects do not demonstrate that God is triune).
claims: God is the subject of theology of necessary truths in itself.
God alone virtually contains all necessary theological truths.
No effect demonstrates the Trinity.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1126.summary: Second proof: this theology concerns what is naturally knowable only to the divine intellect, so its object is naturally known to God alone, and only God is naturally known to himself alone. The infinite divine intellect must have something naturally known only to it, else a higher science would exist, and every created essence is naturally knowable by some created intellect, so what is known to God alone is God himself.
claims: Theology in itself concerns what is naturally knowable only to God.
Only God himself is naturally known to God alone.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1174.summary: Third proof: no science gives as distinct and perfect knowledge of something not its subject as of its subject, since knowing the subject is the intrinsic end of a science. If God were not this science's subject, he could be known more perfectly in another, higher science, which is false, at least of intuitive and abstractive theology in its genus.
claims: A science knows its subject most perfectly.
If God were not theology's subject, a higher science of God would exist.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1198.summary: Fourth proof: the first object of a science is what the science first regards, and everything else through it by likeness or attribution, as colour for sight. In theology of necessary truths, the knower regards God first and other things only through relation to him, both in intuitive theology, whose primary object is the divine essence, and in abstractive theology, whose representative first represents the essence.
claims: In theology the knower regards God first and all else through him.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1229.summary: Fifth proof: the noblest science concerns the noblest genus of being (Metaphysics VI), and theology is the noblest in itself, so it concerns God, the noblest being. If that principle applies to the subject, then, since Aristotle and the Commentator take metaphysics as the noblest acquirable science, separate substances would be the subject of metaphysics, as the Commentator holds; if it applies only to parts or causes of the subject, metaphysics can treat separate substances as causes or parts of its subject, being. But theology is simply noblest, intuitive and abstractive each in its genus, so it must concern the noblest as subject, not merely as part or cause. Metaphysics is not simply noblest, only perhaps the noblest naturally acquirable science.
claims: Theology, being simply noblest, must have the noblest being as its subject.
Metaphysics is at most the noblest naturally acquirable science.
The nobility of a science depends on its object.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1319.summary: Sixth proof: the first object of a science is that to which alone its principal properties belong, as induction over theology's properties shows. This concludes the argument for theology of necessary truths.
claims: Theology's principal properties belong to God alone.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1335.summary: On theology of contingent truths, reports a view (Scotus) that no object determinately contains such truths by its nature, since everything in God stands indifferently and contingently to them or their opposites. Only necessary truths are determinately and virtually contained in an object.
claims: No object determinately contains contingent truths by its nature.
God's nature is indifferent to contingent truths.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1364.summary: The view continues: since contingent truths are ordered and there is a first contingent truth, the first subject of contingent theology is that of which the predicate of the first contingent truth is first and immediately said, whatever that truth is.
claims: The subject of contingent theology is the subject of the first contingent truth.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1386.summary: It is said that the subject of the first contingent truth is naturally seen first as joined to its predicate, since on this view the first contingent truth is known only by intuition of the extremes.
claims: The first contingent truth is known only by intuition of its terms.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1399.summary: The first intuitable proximate to that in which the predicate of the first contingent truth inheres (as actually contingent, not merely possible) is the divine essence, taken as in necessary theology. They conclude that the subject of all theology in itself, in God and the blessed, is the divine essence as 'this', whose vision is not formally science but simple intellection, virtually science and naturally prior to it.
claims: The divine essence is the subject of all theology in itself.
The beatific vision is simple intellection, virtually but not formally science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1432.summary: Begins criticizing the claim that nothing real in God determinately contains contingent theological truths. God knows determinately from eternity contingent complexes and truths.
claims: God knows contingent truths determinately from eternity.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1444.summary: Continuing: God revealed many contingent truths to prophets, which is possible only through something determinately containing them, since nothing can be determinately known through what does not determinately contain it. So something in God must determinately contain them.
claims: Determinate knowledge requires something determinately containing the truth.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1462.summary: Further: the blessed know determinately many, indeed all, contingent truths of faith already past, which requires something in God containing them determinately in intelligible being, namely the divine essence with the will's determination, which contains them virtually and determinately, not by intuition of the extremes in themselves, since the extremes are indifferent.
claims: The divine will's determination contains contingent truths determinately.
The blessed know contingent truths through God's will's determination.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1491.summary: Second claim criticized: that the first object of contingent theology is the immediate subject of the first contingent truth, and that this is the essence as in necessary theology.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1511.summary: Against it: the essence as prior to the will and its determinations is the subject of necessary theology, and no contingent predicate naturally inheres immediately in it. There is no contingency before the will's determination (the will is the first cause of contingency, as they hold elsewhere), and otherwise contingent truths could be known with certainty through the essence, which is impossible.
claims: The divine will is the first cause of contingency.
The essence as prior to the will cannot be the subject of contingent truths.
concepts: divine will as source of contingency

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1546.summary: Further: the essence as essence cannot determine any contingent predicate to itself, else it would do so naturally and necessarily and abolish contingency; so it cannot be the first and immediate subject of a contingent complex.
claims: If the essence determined contingent predicates, contingency would vanish.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1572.summary: Also against the claim that the first contingent truth is known only by intuition: this holds of God's and the blessed's theology, but not universally, since whatever can be known intuitively can be known abstractively; God could reveal the first contingent truth to a wayfarer, as perhaps with Paul and the prophets. The author's own view, with one doctor: the divine essence as essence, prior to the will's determination, is the ratio for knowing all quiddities and necessary complexes, and so the subject of necessary theology. As actually existing under the will's determination of contingents, it is the ratio of knowing contingent complexes with certainty. Among these there is only an accidental order caused by the will's determination, which inheres first and immediately in the divine will as its act. 'The will wills something contingent' is the first and immediate contingent truth, which cannot be known to inhere before it does.
claims: The first contingent truth can be known abstractively by revelation, not only intuitively.
The essence prior to the will is the subject of necessary theology; under the will's determination it grounds contingent knowledge.
Contingent truths have only an accidental order, caused by the divine will.
The first contingent truth is that the divine will determines something contingent.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1686.summary: Concludes: if the first object of contingent theology is the divine will under its determination, it determinately contains the contingents. If it need not determinately contain them (not being science), the essence prior to the will can be the object, or the essence as following the will and representing its determination, containing contingents secondarily and representatively. Contingents are never objects of science properly speaking, only of determinate, certain cognition. Objection: two primary objects would mean two sciences in God, two Words, four persons, and two acts in the blessed, contrary to Augustine's 'single glance'. Reply: there is only one first object simply speaking; the will is first only relatively, as what first determinately contains contingents.
claims: Contingent truths are not objects of science in the strict sense.
There is only one first object simply in God's knowledge; the will is first only relatively for contingents.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1810.summary: On theology for us of necessary truths, reports Scotus: in knowledge not evident from the object one need not assign an object virtually containing its truths or their evidence. Our theology is such, so its first subject suffices to be what is first known, of which the first necessary truth of our theology is immediately known, namely infinite being, the most perfect concept we can have of God.
claims: Non-evident knowledge need not have an object that virtually contains its truths.
Infinite being is the first subject of our theology and our most perfect concept of God.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1862.summary: They add that since our theology concerns the same truths as theology in itself, it is assigned the same subject, God, as to containing these truths, though, not being evident to us, it does not contain their evidence for us.
claims: Our theology shares God as subject with theology in itself, as to containment of truths.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1880.summary: Against the objection that God then would not be a subject, they say that though he gives no evidence, he is subject by virtually containing the truths.
claims: God is subject of our theology by virtual containment, not evidence.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1891.summary: The author does not grant these claims. First, the claim that non-evident knowledge need have no object virtually containing its truths (continued next).

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1904.summary: Against it: faith lacks evidence from the object, yet God must be assigned as its object, virtually containing all its necessary truths, and he contains their evidence for himself. So the claim is not universally true, of faith or of the science of faith, our theology.
claims: Faith, though non-evident, has God as object virtually containing its truths.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1925.summary: On infinite being: it follows that God must be the subject, since infinite being as to its positive content is only God. Infinity, on Scotus's own view, is not a special attribute but an intrinsic degree, not varying the ratio of the essence, so 'infinite being' as it belongs to God is God.
claims: Infinite being, positively taken, is just God.
Infinity is an intrinsic mode, not a distinct attribute.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e1951.summary: Hence, as God virtually contains these truths, so he contains their evidence, if he were known as in heaven. An intensively infinite being virtually contains whatever it can cause, and God, omnipotent, can cause these truths and their knowledge in a created intellect. That 'infinite being' is our most perfect concept of God is very doubtful: the concept of deity seems more perfect, since a univocal concept of being, found in creatures, is compossible with imperfection, while deity is incompossible with all imperfection.
claims: God, as infinite, virtually contains the evidence of theological truths.
The concept of deity is at least as perfect as that of infinite being.
The univocal concept of being is compossible with creaturely imperfection.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2001.summary: Considers a reply: 'infinite being' is incompatible with imperfection even if 'being' is not. The author rejects this, since infinity as an intrinsic degree does not remove the concept's compossibility or add formal repugnance, not varying the concept; but he leaves it as doubtful. He grants God is the subject as to virtual containment, and that our theology is not evident, nor science properly, but says the rejected claims need not follow. He announces proofs that God is the first subject of our theology of necessary truths.
claims: An intrinsic degree does not change a concept's compossibility.
God is the subject of our theology by virtual containment.
Our theology is not science in the strict sense.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2049.summary: First proof: faith and the science by which faith is begotten, nourished, defended, and strengthened (Augustine, De trinitate XIV.1, our theology) have the same first object; God is the first object of faith, as induction over the articles shows.
claims: Faith and theology share the same first object, God.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2067.summary: Second proof: the science perfecting the superior portion of reason has an eternal first subject, since the eternal cannot reduce to the non-eternal; our theology of necessary truths perfects the superior portion in this state; so its subject is eternal, God.
claims: Our theology perfects the superior portion of reason, which concerns the eternal.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2100.summary: Third proof: Augustine (De trinitate XIV.1) says our theology is in part wisdom, chiefly theology of necessary truths, so it concerns formally and first something eternal, which is only God.
claims: Theology is in part wisdom concerning the eternal.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2114.summary: Fourth proof: this science is nobler than others in via, not by greater evidence of demonstration, so by a nobler subject, which is God; one science is nobler by certainty or by the excellence of its object (De anima I).
claims: Theology's superiority comes from its subject, not its certainty.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2134.summary: Fifth proof: the earlier reason about theology in itself can be adduced.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2139.summary: Sixth proof: the subject of a science is that to which its attributes belong; the primary theological attributes (being triune and one) belong first to God.
claims: Theology's primary attributes, such as triunity, belong first to God.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2155.summary: On our theology of contingent truths: its first object is the same as that of theology in itself regarding the same contingents, since it concerns the same truths, though not evidently. Inevidence does not require another subject, any more than for necessary theology, and God as subject of contingent theology in itself does not virtually and determinately contain all its truths.
claims: Our theology of contingents has the same subject as theology of contingents in itself.
Inevidence does not alter the subject of a science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2188.summary: Reports a doctor (Scotus) who holds God is the subject of both necessary and contingent theology, but of contingent theology not as virtually and determinately containing its truths, rather as the first intuitable proximate to the divine will, in which the first contingent predicate inheres. The author notes that the essence would then be subject as concomitant with the will's act, not absolutely. On this view the subject need not make the truths evident nor contain them determinately, since contingents are not properly objects of science, and even in beatific vision contingent truths are evident only from seeing the will's determination. If that suffices, the author observes, the earlier rejected opinion that God absolutely is theology's subject for any intellect could be sustained; he leaves the choice of formulation to the reader.
claims: For contingent theology God is subject as the intuitable proximate to the divine will.
Contingent truths are evident only through the will's determination, even in vision.
On this account God can be held the subject of all theology absolutely.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2308.summary: Third article: excludes opinions. First, that the Word is theology's subject: impossible, since some truths concern the Father, some the Spirit, some all three, so not all reduce to the Word; the three persons are quasi-parts of the subject, though not properly parts. For the same reason the whole Christ cannot be the subject, as some hold, since truths about the Father generating, the Spirit proceeding, and the whole Trinity cannot be attributed to Christ. Christ includes created human nature, essentially posterior to the Father, Spirit, and Trinity.
claims: The Word cannot be the subject of theology, since not all truths reduce to the Word.
The whole Christ cannot be the subject, since he includes created nature and Trinitarian truths are not attributable to him.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2368.summary: Excludes a second opinion: 'the credible' taken commonly for all theology treats cannot be its subject, since such a common notion cannot virtually contain theological attributes and truths, as shown for 'divine being' in common. Nothing but God can be the first subject of theology.
claims: 'The credible' in common cannot be the subject of theology.
Only God can be theology's first subject.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2390.summary: Reply to the first argument of the 'divine being' opinion: the first subject need not contain everything by universality of predication, but by virtual containment, as far as possible; indeed predicative universality is impossible in theology.
claims: The subject contains its science virtually, not by predicative universality.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2412.summary: Reply to the second: whether or not God is the immediate subject of metaphysics (the author thinks not), he could still be theology's subject, since diverse sciences can concern the same object under the same ratio. Science takes its unity from the object in that a single science requires a single object, but this does not suffice, so one subject can have several sciences differentiated otherwise.
claims: Several sciences can share a subject.
A single object is necessary but not sufficient for a science's unity.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2438.summary: To answer fully: God is not the immediate subject of metaphysics, against Averroes, who also says metaphysics does not prove God's existence but physics does. Against that: a subject is unprovable because of its primacy, and it would have greater or equal primacy relative to a posterior science, so if metaphysics (simply prior) cannot demonstrate God, physics cannot. If physics demonstrated metaphysics' subject, it would demonstrate its first principle and be prior to it. And any property depending on a cause proves the cause; metaphysical properties (with imperfections dependent on the supreme perfect) do so as well as motion, so the metaphysician proves God as well as or better than the physicist.
claims: God is not the immediate subject of metaphysics.
If metaphysics cannot prove its subject, physics cannot either.
The metaphysician proves God's existence as well as or better than the physicist.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2497.summary: Both Averroes and his opponents are wrong: a science can demonstrate its subject's existence a posteriori (quia), even perhaps propter quid, as to actual existence, not the quidditative possibility presupposed of it. With Avicenna, the author holds God is not the subject of metaphysics or any naturally acquired science, since such a subject must be immediately knowable via sense, while God's most proper feature (being supreme or greatest being) is known only by comparison and discursive reasoning.
claims: A science can demonstrate its subject's actual existence a posteriori.
God is not the subject of any naturally acquired science.
The subject of a natural science must be immediately knowable from sense.
concepts: knowledge of God through discursive reasoning

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2530.summary: Reply to the third: power relates to object differently than science to subject. The object relates to a power as mover to mobile, and one mobile can have several unordered movers, so a power's adequate object must be common. A science's subject is its cause and measure, virtually containing it, and one measured effect cannot have several unordered total causes, so the subject must be one, not a common predicable. Sciences assigned common subjects (being for metaphysics, mobile being for physics) are one only generically or by order, or their subjects lack two conditions (measuring and virtually containing) while having the third (terminating). Also, a power has wider scope than a science.
claims: A power's object is a mover; a science's subject is a cause and measure.
A science's subject must be one, not a common predicate.
Sciences with common subjects are unified only generically, or their subjects are incomplete.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2609.summary: Reply to the fourth: in a way a science does prove its subject, as shown. Reply to the fifth (subalternation): the argument would make all sciences subalternate to metaphysics, since all subjects fall under being. Subalternation requires taking principles from another science, as optics from geometry, which theology does not do from metaphysics, proceeding from its own principles.
claims: Subalternation requires borrowing principles, not merely containment of subjects.
Theology is not subalternate to metaphysics, since it proceeds from its own principles.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2640.summary: Reply to the sixth: it shows only that God cannot be the subject of a naturally acquired science, not of revealed sciences, such as our theology or higher theology, which need not have a subject first known and immediately had from sense. Alternatively, the subject need not be first known simply, only as subject in that science, and its knowledge can come from another known object, as substance presupposes knowledge of accidents.
claims: God can be the subject of revealed sciences, though not of natural ones.
A subject need be first known only within its science, not simply.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2671.summary: Reply to the first principal argument (Boethius): a utterly simple form like God cannot be a subject in the sense of perfectible by something to which it is in potency, which would make it composite; but it can be the subject about which a science is, which posits nothing received in it and is consistent with total simplicity.
claims: God cannot be a receptive subject but can be the subject-matter of a science.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2691.summary: Reply to the second: matter as part of a composite does not coincide with end and efficient cause, but matter 'about which' as object can, and God is such matter of this science, not distinguishing here matter from subject.
claims: Matter 'about which' can coincide with efficient and final cause.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2704.summary: Reply to the third: having principles is accidental to a science's object and to demonstration as such, holding only for sciences of caused objects. Or: though God has no principles of being, he has features from which immediate propositions can be formed and things demonstrated of him a priori. Having integral or subjective parts is likewise accidental, belonging to sciences of created objects; or the three persons are quasi-subjective parts of God.
claims: Having principles or parts is accidental to a science's subject.
God has features from which a priori demonstrations about him can be formed.
The three persons are quasi-subjective parts of God.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2748.summary: On attributes: the divine essence has many perfections functioning as quasi-attributes, however they are distinguished, sufficient for true demonstration.
claims: Divine perfections serve as quasi-attributes for demonstration.

qrdBas-ae6817-d1e2758.summary: Reply to the last: God has no definitional 'what it is', since strict definition is by genus and difference and would limit him; but he has a quiddity and a quidditative concept of his essence, which suffices for demonstration and science.
claims: God has no definition by genus and difference.
God has a quiddity and quidditative concept sufficient for science.

qrdBas-ae6817.summary: Prologue q3 asks whether God is the subject of theology. Bassolis first sets out the theory of a science's first subject. It is first known in the science by twofold precognition (meaning and non-impossibility), through its own formal, actual ratio, and virtually contains all the science's knowledge. Relative to the science it specifies, unifies, ennobles, and names it as an extrinsic cause, and grounds its principles. He compares the objects of powers and of habits: powers have common adequate objects as movers, while a science's subject is its cause and measure and must be one, with primacy of both immediacy and adequation. He also explains how 'subject' and 'matter' apply to a science. Against the view that the subject is 'divine being' in common, he argues that only God properly (that to which deity belongs quidditatively) virtually contains the theological truths. Distinguishing theology in itself (evident, apt for a proportioned intellect) from theology for us, and necessary from contingent truths, he proves by six arguments that God is the subject of necessary theology. For contingent theology, against a view (Scotus's) that nothing in God determinately contains contingents, he holds that the divine will under its determination is relatively first, the first contingent truth being that the will wills something, and that such truths can be revealed abstractively. Against Scotus's 'infinite being' as subject of our theology, he argues that infinite being positively is just God and that the concept of deity is at least as perfect. He excludes the Word, the whole Christ, and 'the credible' as subjects. He denies (against Averroes) that God is the subject of metaphysics or that physics alone proves God, holding with Avicenna that God is the subject of no naturally acquired science, and that theology is not subalternate to metaphysics.
claims: The first subject of a science is first known, virtually contains all its truths, and specifies it as extrinsic cause.
God (that to which deity belongs quidditatively) is the subject of theology, both in itself and for us.
For contingent theology, the divine will under its determination is the relatively first object; contingents are not objects of science strictly.
Infinite being, as positive content, is simply God; the concept of deity is no less perfect.
Neither the Word, the whole Christ, divine being in common, nor the credible is theology's subject.
God is not the subject of metaphysics or any natural science; theology is not subalternate to metaphysics.
concepts: theology in itself and for us
